title: Tesla's real disruption wasn't electric — it rewrote the auto industry's rules
dek: Legacy automakers didn't miss Tesla; they filed it as a new toy in a niche segment. What actually got disrupted was the seven-year model cycle, the dealer system and supply-chain interests — baggage that kept them from turning around.
why: An executive who spent over a decade at Mercedes, Aston Martin and Jaguar Land Rover explains that what foreign automakers missed wasn't technology, it was the rules. The second half on going overseas and management is especially valuable.
who: Founders and investors watching auto exports, foreign brands' China strategy and cross-border organizational management — especially Chinese brand teams entering or preparing to enter the North American market.
skip: 1:02:15 to 1:09:10 on Canadian charging piles and Tesla exporting from Shanghai — low information density.

points.h: Tesla was filed as a new toy in a niche segment
points.body: Freda revisits how Mercedes judged it at the time: legacy automakers didn't miss Tesla, they categorized it as ‘a new product in a niche segment’, a functional replacement for one powertrain. Back then luxury customers said buying a Tesla was a status symbol, an innovation label, and Mercedes' reaction was — you have five or six cars in your garage, adding one more is fine, you won't drift far from the traditional luxury brand. The error in that judgment was failing to realize that EVs opened up a new business model and redefined the automobile product. She draws a Kodak analogy: when digital cameras came out, Kodak also thought they might be a new toy for enthusiasts.

points.h: Direct sales is only the most superficial change
points.body: Freda says Tesla was the first brand to switch from dealer sales to direct sales, the most obvious change from the customer side, but behind it are bigger things: changes in suppliers and the supply chain, and changes in the speed of new-car development. These were only realized later. She stresses that legacy automakers realized Tesla was taking customers and having an effect in the market, but ‘still didn't fully realize whether EV would change the competitive rules of the auto industry’.

points.h: Turning a ship of hundreds of thousands is hard in process, not awareness
points.body: Freda says legacy automakers weren't unaware that digitalization was needed, but ‘a company of hundreds of thousands, such a big ship turning around to make this change, the process is extremely, extremely difficult’. At the time sales were doubling every year, dealers could open 50 new stores a year, and digitization was like a new initiative, a new campaign, done from headquarters to regions, but resistance was huge and the process long. She gives the example of official websites: many brands' websites are still centrally controlled by headquarters today, while Chinese consumers' online interaction habits are more sophisticated and they need more information — this communication process is very long.

points.h: Global consistency overrides Chinese consumer needs
points.body: Freda explains why headquarters are reluctant to delegate: branding has always been about global consistency. Luxury brands especially insist ‘you can't follow trends, trends may pass in the blink of an eye’, and must stick to brand tonality and a globally consistent look and feel. The official website is absolutely not up for grabs; only China-specific platforms like mini-programs can the China team use to persuade headquarters. But even then, headquarters needs to be persuaded to let go — every time headquarters visits they ask why the materials headquarters gave you can't be used in China, why you need Xiaohongshu. She says such questions are ‘pretty dumb’, but the China team still has to persuade them every day.

points.h: A century-old rulebook disrupted by six-month iteration
points.body: Freda says the gasoline car industry has been in Germany for over a hundred years, many brands are over a hundred years old, and the rules were set by these players over a century. In the past Chinese, Korean and Japanese brands all entered and played by these rules: car updates were a seven-year generation major facelift and a five-year minor facelift, and that's how it was for decades. But today an EV might come out with a new feature every six months, and won't let your process run — ‘the entire auto industry's rules are completely disrupted’. Her personal judgment is that legacy automakers haven't realized how revolutionary the change is.

points.h: Supply chain and dealers are baggage they can't carry
points.body: Freda breaks down why legacy automakers can't turn around: German companies have Tier 1 and Tier 2 suppliers behind them, with decades of cooperation with the brand — it's not like you don't need engines this year and can cut them tomorrow; the dealer system has been formed for so many years, protecting dealer profitability is a rule everyone must follow, and a brand can't say I don't care about five or six hundred dealers, I'll sell directly to consumers. Chinese new EV brands entered as EVs from the start, could set their own rules, could go half dealers half direct sales, ‘without so much baggage’. Legacy automakers carry countless burdens, and it can't change overnight.

points.h: 2023 Shanghai Auto Show: BYD put Yangwang next to Mercedes
points.body: Freda says the 2023 Shanghai Auto Show was the first after the pandemic; in the past foreign Global CEOs and global R&D presidents would come to China several times a year, but during those years visas were hard and quarantine was required, so visits dropped a lot, causing a huge surprise in 2023. She checked the data: in 2023 there were about 100, 130, 150 new products, of which Chinese brands accounted for 100, and 70% were pure electric. At the auto show, which hall and what position matters a lot; luxury brands are all together, and BBA each bring a luxury brand. But that year, for the first time, BYD put Yangwang next to Mercedes, in the same hall, and began the high-end positioning of domestic brands.

points.h: Betting on gasoline, hybrid and EV at once — where's the focus?
points.body: Freda says this is a huge strategic question she hasn't figured out: EV companies like NIO, Li Auto and XPeng only have EVs and hybrids to invest in, but legacy automakers have gasoline cars, hybrids and EVs, and must also invest in R&D and new product production, with limited capital — where is the focus? Worse, China is in a state of EVs running forward, while Europe relaxed standards and the US and Canada completely withdrew EV sales subsidies; only China, such a large market, is moving fast. She believes these foreign companies in China today ‘please no one and do no product well’.

points.h: Going overseas, the scarcest talent is someone who can talk to dealer investors
points.body: Freda says the first requirement for Chinese brands looking for people overseas is to screen for Chinese who can talk to local dealer investors. The reason is that Chinese companies need local middle management who can both talk to them and understand the Chinese brand's business thinking, and also connect with local dealers and speak their language. But such talent ‘you can probably count on one hand’ — there are many Chinese, but not many who sit in this position and can communicate on equal footing with dealer investors. From this she raises a bigger concern: Chinese companies going overseas also face the headquarters-region relationship, and should not repeat the path foreign companies took in the Chinese market.

points.h: What Chinese companies lack most is multicultural management and compliance
points.body: Freda says the management experience and corporate culture cultivated by foreign companies, especially compliance, are highly valued by both American and German companies, and these have not been trained in other markets and companies. Conversely, what Chinese companies lack most now is actually management, especially multicultural management, and the concept of compliance — respect for different cultures, which is the most basic entry-level thing for running a company, but is not particularly emphasized domestically. So people coming from headquarters don't have this concept in some places, creating a mismatch, with different expectations and different requirements between local teams and headquarters.
